books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant, 1913

stimulus.text: The photograph shows a row of Model T chassis — frames with wheels, engines, and steering wheels, but no bodies — moving along a conveyor line inside a large factory hall at Ford's Highland Park plant in 1913. Overhead belts and wheels drive the line. No workers are visible in this view.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, Assembly line at the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park plant, 1913, Library of Congress LCCN2011661021, public domain.

rationales.A: Westward expansion filled the continent in the 1800s. The 1920s boom came from factories, not new land.
rationales.B: Wartime cooperation collapsed when the Senate rejected the League. The consumer economy was a domestic industrial change.
rationales.C: Mass production made goods cheap and standard, so ordinary families could buy cars, radios, and appliances. The assembly line is the cause the photo shows.
rationales.D: The government did not limit factory output in the 1920s. Output rose, and easy credit helped buyers absorb it.
rationales.general:
1. Connect the photo to the decade: the line made cars fast and cheap.
2. Widen the view: the same methods made radios and appliances cheap, too.
3. Add the buyers: easy credit and advertising turned cheap goods into a consumer economy.
Remember: to find the root of a boom, follow the price down to the method that cut it.
